method.label: Method
method.definition: name of the measurement method or distance indicator

principle.label: Principle
principle.definition: the fundamental physical basis that provides the cosmological information relevant to the determination of $H_0$

data_product.label: Data Product
data_product.definition: observational representation from which the relevant physical quantities are extracted

physical_quantities.label: Physical Quantity
physical_quantities.definition: physical quantity inferred or measured from the observational data

h0_inference_route.label: $H_0$ Inference Route
h0_inference_route.definition: how the measured information contributes to the inference of $H_0$

redshift_range.label: Redshift Range
redshift_range.definition: redshift range directly used in published $H_0$ measurements or inferences when available; otherwise, the forecast redshift range for methods not yet applied to $H_0$ measurements

cosmic_epoch.label: Cosmic Epoch
cosmic_epoch.definition: the cosmic epoch reached by observations used in an $H_0$ measurement or inference, classified according to the maximum redshift used

cosmological_model_dependence.label: Cosmological Model Dependence
cosmological_model_dependence.definition: degree to which the inference relies on assumptions about cosmological physics or expansion history

observation_role.label: Observation Role
observation_role.definition: whether an observation defines the principal target or supports it

entries.definition: absolute distance is derived from the geometry/dynamics of an individual system
a physical length scale is known, standardised or calibrated rather than being determined from the individual system
the intrinsic luminosity is known, standardised or calibrated
absolute luminosity distance is inferred from the gravitational-wave signal
an absolute age or a standardisable differential age interval is inferred from astrophysical evolution
cosmological path-length or expansion information is encoded in a propagation effect accumulated along the line of sight
constrains a cosmological distance, which encodes the expansion history through an integral, and $H_0$ is obtained using the distance-redshift relation
constrains the expansion rate $H(z)$ directly, $H_0$ is inferred by extrapolating or fitting the expansion history to $z=0$
a physical effect is accumulated along the line of sight whose redshift dependence encodes cosmological path-length or expansion information, from which $H_0$ is inferred
the observed data are compared with predictions from a full cosmological model, where $H_0$ is obtained simultaneously with other cosmological parameters through a global model fit
a system whose distance is determined geometrically and is used to calibrate the absolute scale of the first-rung indicator
a nearby indicator calibrated by geometric anchors, which is used to measure distances to more distant galaxies hosting second-rung indicators and thereby calibrate the second rung
a more distant-reaching indicator calibrated by the first rung, which extends into the Hubble flow and is used to infer $H_0$ through the D-z relation
no specific dynamical cosmological model is required; relies only on FLRW kinematics / local cosmography
requires assumptions about the late-time expansion history or externally constrained $\Omega_b$
uses a physical scale from pre-recombination physics
directly fits observables generated by early-universe physics using a detailed cosmological model
defines the method's principal astronomical target and is used for method discovery/filtering
supporting observation, such as host-galaxy redshift measurement, which is retained in the full observation chain but is not used as a primary target filter

distance_ladder.label: distance ladder
distance_ladder.definition: In the distance ladder, each rung is calibrated using overlapping objects with the previous rung, allowing the absolute distance scale to be propagated to increasingly distant galaxies. Once a distance indicator is calibrated, it is applied to more distant galaxies to obtain luminosity distances and host-galaxy redshifts. The resulting distance–redshift relation, usually represented by a Hubble diagram, is then used to determine the Hubble constant $H_0$.
